title: SEBI - 0367/2004 — Shubam & Co. v. Securities and Exchange Board of India
text:
IN THE SECURITIES APPELLATE TRIBUNAL
MUMBAI
Appeal No. 367 of 2004
Date of decision : 15th February, 2007
Shubam & Co. .. .. Appellant
Versus
Securities and Exchange Board of India .. .. Respondent
Mr. Bharat Merchant , Advocate for the appellant.
Dr. Poornima Advani, Advocate with Ms. Sejal Shah along with Mr. U.N.
Das, Advocate for the respondent.
Coram : Justice N.K. Sodhi, Presiding Officer
R.N. Bhardwaj, Member
Per : Justice N.K. Sodhi, Presiding Officer
Challenge in this appeal is to the order dated August 17, 2004 passed
by the adjudicating officer imposing a penalty of Rs.1,60,000/- on Shubam
& Co.– appellant herein for violating the provisions of sections 15A(c ) and
15B of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 (for short the
Act). The facts giving rise to this appeal lie in a narrow compass and these
may first be noticed.
The appellant before us is a registered stock broker. By letter dated
September 13, 2002, the Securities and Exchange Board of India
(hereinafter referred to as the Board) appointed J.N. Sharma & Co.,
chartered accountants to carry out inspection of the books of account and

2
short comings in the books of account, records and systems of accounting
as maintained by the appellant and submitted its report dated 30th October,
2002 to the Board. Since the penalty has been imposed on the appellant on
two counts, we shall refer to those discrepancies only. On receipt of the
inspection report, a copy of the same was forwarded to the appellant and it
was required to send its comments along with documentary evidence on the
irregularities mentioned in the report. The appellant furnished its
comments as per its letter dated 3.3.3003, in which it stated as under –
“1(iii) Order Book have not been maintained properly, but in
this context, we have to inform you that we have only few
clients and they are either relative or close friends of the
proprietor. But we assure you to maintain proper order book in
future. SEBI Auditor checked the Sauda Book, hence this
allegation is denied.”
On a consideration of inspection report and the comments offered by the
appellant, the Board decided to initiate adjudication proceedings and
appointed an adjudicating officer on December 5, 2003 to inquire into and
adjudge the alleged contravention of, amongst others, sections 15A(c ) and
15B of the Act by the appellant for its failure to maintain statutory books of
account and records and its failure to enter into agreements with its clients.
The adjudicating officer served the appellant with a notice dated January 8,
2004 to show cause why an inquiry be not held against it for the alleged
contravention of the statutory provisions referred to therein. The reply

3
conclusion that the appellant had not maintained the “order” book and that
the “sauda” book did not contain the particulars of orders received from the
clients. He also found that there was no record kept by the appellant to
show the date and time of receiving the orders, name and number of scrips
ordered and other necessary instructions, if any, received from the clients.
The adjudicating officer further concluded that it was not possible to verify
whether all orders received by the appellant had been executed and, if not,
the reasons for non-execution and whether the orders were executed in
accordance with the instructions issued by the clients. The adjudicating
officer relied upon the admission made by the appellant in this regard and
observed that the appellant did not have the practice of executing
agreements with its clients. It appears that during the course of adjudication
proceedings the appellant made available some agreements allegedly
executed with its clients and since those were not executed on stamp paper
it was not possible to establish the actual date of their execution. He also
observed that unstamped agreements could not be enforced in a court of
law and, therefore, they did not offer adequate protection to the investor
whose interests have to be protected by the Board. He, thus, found that
section 15B of the Act also stood violated. By his order dated August 17,
2004, the adjudicating officer imposed the penalty as stated in the earlier
part of the order. Hence this appeal.
We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and find no merit
in the appeal. The fact that the appellant had not maintained “order” book

4
earlier part of the order where the appellant admitted that it had not
maintained the order book but assured the Board that it would be
maintained properly in future. In view of this admission the charge
levelled against the appellant stands established. What is contended by the
learned counsel for the appellant is that the rules and regulations framed
under the Act do not require a stock broker to maintain “order” book. We
can not accept this contention. The learned counsel for the respondent
placed before us a copy of the circular dated February 11, 1997 issued by
the Board to all the stock exchanges in the country and registered market
intermediaries and drew our attention to clause 7 thereof which provides
that a “broker member should maintain record of time when the client has
placed the order and reflect the same in contract note along with the time of
execution of the order.” As per this circular which is binding on all the
market intermediaries including the appellant, stock brokers are required to
maintain some record where time when the client places an order must be
recorded and the same should be reflected in the contract note along with
the time of execution of the order. Admittedly, the appellant has not been
maintaining any such record which is usually maintained in a register
commonly known as order book. Clause 7 of the circular may appear to be
innocuous but it is not so and is a very important step which the board has
taken to protect the interests of the investors. In a volatile market like ours
where the price of a scrip fluctuates every moment, it is absolutely
necessary that a broker should record the time when it receives an order
from the client and also the time when the same is executed. If this is not

5
mandatory for the stock brokers to maintain such records. Having issued
the circular, the Board would be well advised in ensuring strict compliance
thereof by every stock broker so that the interests of the investors do not get
jeopardised..
As regards non-execution of the agreement with its clients, it may be
mentioned that law requires every stock broker to execute an agreement
with his client (s) and provides a severe penalty for not doing so. When the
records of the appellant were inspected by the chartered accountants, the
former did not produce the agreements before them and, therefore, the
inspecting team was right in observing that the appellant did not have the
practice of executing agreements with its clients. However, during the
course of adjudication proceedings the appellant produced some
agreements allegedly executed with its clients and those agreements were
not on stamp paper and the adjudicating officer was right in not relying
upon those agreements because it is not possible to establish the actual date
of their execution. The agreements were apparently an after thought and
were prepared by the appellant for the purpose of adjudication proceedings.
In this view of the matter, we cannot find any fault with the finding
recorded by the adjudicating officer. We are, therefore, satisfied that
section 15B of the Act also stood violated.
In view of the serious irregularities committed by the appellant and
also in view of the fact that sections 15A (c ) and 15B of the Act stood

6
Chairman, SEBI v Shriram Mutual Fund AIR 2006 SC 2287 wherein their
lordships observed as under –
In our considered opinion, penalty is attracted as soon as the
contravention of the statutory obligation as contemplated by the Act
and the Regulation is established and hence the intention of the
parties committing such violation becomes wholly irrelevant. A
breach of civil obligation which attracts penalty in the nature of fine
under the provisions of the Act and the Regulations would
immediately attract the levy of penalty irrespective of the fact
whether contravention must made by the defaulter with guilty
intention or not. We also further held that unless the language of the
statute indicates the need to establish the presence of mens rea, it is
wholly unnecessary to ascertain whether such a violation was
intentional or not. On a careful perusal of Section 15(D)(b) and
Section 15E of the Act, there is nothing which requires that mens rea
must be proved before penalty can be imposed under these
provisions. Hence once the contravention is established then the
penalty is to follow.”
Section 15A of the Act before its amendment by the amending Act of 2002
provided that for the violation of clause (c ) thereof, a penalty not
exceeding ten thousand rupees for every day during which the failure
continues could be imposed. Similarly, section 15B of the Act before its

7
with its clients. Having regard to the period during which the failure
continued and the amount of penalty prescribed by the Act we are of the
view that penalty of Rs.1,60,000/- imposed by the adjudicating officer is
more than reasonable and does not call for any inference by us in appeal.
In the result, the appeal fails and the same is dismissed with no order
as to the costs.
Justice N.K. Sodhi
Presiding Officer
R.N. Bhardwaj
Member
Date : 15. 2. 2007
BBN
respondent: Securities and Exchange Board of India
